articles.title: Explosive sleeper issue could fuel midterm shakeups, top Republican predicts: ‘You’re gonna see surprises’
articles.summary: Tom Emmer says fraud is the top issue driving Minnesota voters to the polls and predicts Republican "surprises" in several midterm elections.
articles.body: LEWISTON, MAINE - With just about a month left until the midterm elections, Rep. Tom Emmer (R-MN) told Fox News Digital that fraud is an issue motivating voters to the polls, and in Minnesota, his home state, he thinks the issue could yield some "surprises" at the ballot box. "Fraud is a lot more important to the U.S. taxpayers than being a Republican or a Democrat," Emmer said. "People want good government. They want to know that they're paying for good government, that they are not having their hard-earned taxpayer dollars being siphoned off and stolen and sent out of the country. They're also asking, why hasn't anyone called this out and held these people accountable? And I think you're going to see that at the ballot box on November 3." Emmer, the House Majority Whip, was in Maine with Republican House candidate Paul LePage, the first stop of his planned 56-district nationwide blitz across the United States, rallying voters for Republicans as the party tries to hold on their razor-thin majority in the House against daunting historical and political headwinds. Emmer’s home state of Minnesota was the epicenter of fraud’s explosion into the national conversation late last year, prompting Gov. Tim Walz to abandon his re-election bid. Emmer expressed optimism that Republicans in Minnesota will resonate with voters on fraud in a state where a Republican hasn’t won a statewide election since 2006. KLOBUCHAR'S FRAUD FIGHT CLAIM TAKES HIT AFTER GOP OPPONENT COMBS THROUGH RECEIPTS: 'WHERE WERE YOU?' "Fraud in Minnesota is the number one issue," Emmer said. "We've got a completely incompetent, I would argue corrupt in some instances, governor and an attorney general who took campaign funds from Somali fraudsters that he was actively trying to protect from getting caught in their fraud. This is a big deal for Minnesotans." Emmer said voters are looking for an "honest system that actually works for the people" and not "the criminals" and the Republican candidates for Senate, governor, attorney general and auditor in Minnesota have all made fighting fraud a central issue of their campaigns. NEW AUDIT IN WALZ'S BACKYARD EXPOSES MASSIVE FRAUD RISK TIED TO POST-GEORGE FLOYD ACTIVISM "You easily could have Michelle Tafoya being the next U.S. Senator from the state of Minnesota, a Republican, you could have Lisa Demuth as the Republican governor and already, the attorney general candidate, Ron Schutz and the state auditor candidate Scott Jensen, the polling showing that they are leading," Emmer said. "So yes, Minnesota is going to be one of those places where you see surprises. I think you're gonna see surprises in Michigan as well and other places all across the country." Emmer sat down for a roundtable discussion on fraud with LePage, Maine’s former governor running for Congress in the state’s 2nd Congressional District, where the Minnesota Republican railed against the lack of accountability for fraud in his home state. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "They need to be held accountable and that's the one thing that's missing again in Minnesota. You've got all of these fraudsters being charged and convicted, not one public official has been charged at all, and that's got to change, and I hope it changes in Maine and other places, because it's high time that people be held accountable for ripping off the generous American people," Emmer told the panel. The Trump administration has made combating fraud a central focus this year, creating a Justice Department Fraud Division and a White House task force led by Vice President JD Vance. The White House says the task force has uncovered roughly $245.7 billion in fraud since its creation, while also stopping an additional $62.9 billion annually and enforcing $59.1 billion through criminal charges, settlements and penalties.

articles.title: Trump DOJ investigating Dem group in Texas after viral undercover video sparks massive uproar
articles.summary: A viral undercover video showing a Texas Majority PAC employee describing a "Paid Relational Program" has now triggered a DOJ investigation.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: A Texas PAC that dumps millions into Democrat campaigns in the Lone Star state is under a Department of Justice (DOJ) investigation following a viral undercover video featuring a now-former employee, two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to Fox News Digital. "We are paying people $25 to attend a one-hour Zoom class to learn why voting is important and why the Republicans are causing all these bad things," Sky McAdams, a former organizing manager at the Texas Majority PAC told an undercover reporter in a video obtained by Townhall. "So it's like a roundabout way of paying people for their votes, essentially, which is interesting," said McAdams. When the undercover reporter asked what the program was called, McAdams said it's called the "Paid Relational Program." "I think 'Rally Texas' is the official name," McAdams continued. "You can't pay someone to vote for someone. You can't be like, 'Here's $25, go vote for me.' You can say, 'attend a one-hour class and you can receive $25,' and then the class just talks about, like, the importance of voting." REPUBLICAN CAVALRY ARRIVES FOR KEN PAXTON AS BIG-BUCKS TEXAS OFFENSIVE OPENS CASH FLOODGATES "It's a creative way to kind of... but right now we could use all the help we can get," the reporter says in response. "Yeah, you know, like, if I was a Republican, I'd be pissed. I'd be like, 'that's shady as f---,'" McAdams agreed of the supposed nefarious-ness of the action in his reply. The video has racked up millions of views online, leading to the DOJ probe into the Texas Majority PAC. The Texas Majority PAC was founded by "veterans of Texas campaigns" Jason Lee, Katherine Fischer and Crystal Zermeño. The group's mission is to turn Texas permanently blue. According to Transparency USA, by the end of Q2, the PAC had raised nearly $10 million in the 2026 election cycle, and has spent nearly $9 million. It reportedly had more than $1.3 million in cash on hand. A spokesperson for the PAC, Eddie Vale, told Fox News Digital that the video is real and has not been digitally altered or deceptively edited. He also clarified details about "relational organizing" program described by McAdams in the video. TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS "We hire Texans to join events where they are taught how to organize their friends and family.," he said. "They encourage their friends and family to turn out and vote and send them regular reminders. They are compensated for their organizing work, just like any other job." "Texas Majority PAC runs a relational organizing program, which for years has been a standard part of every campaign’s playbook," Vale said. "Participants in the program are being paid for grassroots organizing work. The way it was described by one rogue employee is factually incorrect, not how we operate, and they were immediately fired." "We will continue to ensure that everyone who has the legal right to vote is able to do so in the face of never-ending attempts from Texas Republicans to disenfranchise them and bad faith attacks from right-wing media to silence organizations that try to help them," Vale continued. Meanwhile, Texas Democrats are feverishly attempting to rally support for scandal-plagued Senate candidate James Talarico. The left-wing candidate has recently walked back some of his more extreme positions, like support for biological men in women's sports, his previous claims that "God is non-binary" and that there are six sexes. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Talarico is running against Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton. Despite the fact that Texas is known as a traditionally red state, the outcome could be decided by a razor-thin margin. Neither McAdams nor the Texas Majority PAC returned Fox News Digital's comment requests related to the investigation.

articles.title: GOP lawmaker’s fraud crusade takes dramatic turn as scandal engulfs his own career
articles.summary: Utah State Rep. Trevor Lee, a Republican who championed anti-fraud bills and praised Nick Shirley, now faces mortgage fraud charges himself.
articles.body: After spending years railing against fraud, Utah Republican state Rep. Trevor Lee has resigned after being charged with fraud himself. The Utah Attorney General's Office filed criminal charges against Lee on Monday, accusing him of forging documents and engaging in fraud in order to obtain a home loan. Prior to the charges, Lee had pushed legislation aimed at combating unemployment fraud and publicly praised efforts to expose the sweeping fraud scandals that have rocked Minnesota in recent years. In one video obtained by prosecutors, the CEO of a Utah water company "stated that Lee had requested cash advances totaling $93,000 to show increased income to assist in purchasing his home, and that Lee said he would make (the CEO) 'whole' by securing (his) company a government contract with Hill Air Force Base," according to the charging document. SWING-STATE'S FRAUD RECKONING RAISES MINNESOTA-STYLE ALARM AS WILD SCHEMES EXPOSED Another company claimed that Lee improperly used an offer letter from them to make it seem as if his income was higher than it was. "Lee devised a scheme to obtain a $1 million home loan by false pretenses. To execute it, he communicated fraudulent documents to Kind Lending through the mortgage process — a forged Enevive employment contract, a loan application overstating his Enevive income, and a Blue Logic offer letter he knew misrepresented his employment," prosecutors wrote. Investigators say Lee admitted during an interview that he personally forged the Enevive CEO’s signature on the employment contract to obtain the loan and knew the offer letter did not reflect income the company could actually pay him. EXCLUSIVE: NICK SHIRLEY FIRES BACK AT MINNESOTA CRITICS: 'NUMBERS DON'T LIE, AND CONVICTIONS DON'T LIE' Lee’s social media feed is full of positive references to Nick Shirley, a content creator who attracted national attention after releasing videos alleging fraud involving Somali-run childcare centers and other publicly funded programs in Minnesota. "Nick is going to stop a Gavin Newsom presidency single handily (sic.)," Lee said in one post. In another post, Lee offered Shirley assistance after he was charged a fee for filming at the Utah state capital building. "Keep up the good work Nick," Lee said in his most recent post directed at the YouTuber, dated July 11. In addition to the praise of Shirley, Lee also introduced pieces of legislation designed to crack down on unemployment assistance fraud in 2023 and 2024. BRAZEN SOCIAL MEDIA FRAUD SCHEMES WREAK HAVOC AS TRUMP OFFICIAL ISSUES STARK WARNING FOR 'FRAUDFLUENCERS' Lee resigned from the legislature shortly after the charges were filed. "Due to personal circumstances that require my attention, I no longer feel I can give my constituents the time, attention and service they deserve," he said. "I will always be grateful for the people I have met, the relationships I have built and the opportunity I have had to serve the people of Utah." Even if the fraud charges hadn’t come, Lee’s time in the legislature was approaching an end as he had lost his GOP primary election in June. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lee did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

articles.title: Schumer tanks popular insider trading ban in Dem effort to derail Republican's agenda ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Senate Democrats blocked a GOP bill combining a stock trading ban with voter ID requirements, with Chuck Schumer calling it "trickery" and "skullduggery."
articles.body: Senate Democrats shut down Republicans’ bid to deal with two key issues for voters heading into the midterms. Republicans tried and failed to pass a bill that would marry differing policy issues: banning lawmakers from using their insider knowledge to trade stocks and implementing voter ID policy nationwide — the latter of which the GOP has so far failed to accomplish with their SAVE America Act. The Stop Insider Trading Act cruised through the House earlier this month, where a majority of House Democrats voted against it. Though voters are highly supportive of both, Democrats in the House and Senate argued that the stock trade ban wasn’t strong enough, while the voter ID element was too aggressive. But the efforts to shut down the votes appear to build on a growing trend ahead of the November midterms — Democrats don't want to hand Republicans two massive wins going into a must-win election for both parties. SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., argued that Republicans knew the bill would never pass, and that they "designed it that way." "They don't want this bill to become law," Schumer insisted. "So they put a poison pill in that they knew would tank it." "It's really trickery. Skullduggery," he added. "If Republican senators really cared about stopping stock trading by members, they wouldn't have loaded it up with a poison pill voter ID bill, which Senate Democrats have defeated already twice." They are two issues, though worlds apart, that have routinely failed to launch in Congress. Senate Democrats have blocked voter ID and the SAVE America Act — and its several iterations throughout the year — multiple times, while banning lawmakers from trading stocks has largely been stifled by intraparty quarrels on both sides of the aisle. SCHUMER SAID ‘DEMOCRATS SUPPORT VOTER ID’ — THEN EVERY SENATE DEMOCRAT VOTED AGAINST GOP BILL House Republicans are unhappy the legislation failed, too. "No lawmaker should be able to profit off of insider information. I’ll continue my work to pass the Stop Insider Trading Act," House Administration Committee Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., told Fox News Digital. "I’m encouraged that 53 Senators voted to ban members of Congress from trading stocks this afternoon. Unfortunately, Senate Democrats filibustered this commonsense ethics reform." Still, they are issues that Americans overwhelmingly support. A poll from the University of Maryland published in 2023 found that 86% of Americans on both sides of the political spectrum supported banning lawmakers from trading stocks. And a 2025 poll from the Pew Research Center found that 83% of Americans favored "requiring all voters to show government-issued photo identification to vote." It’s the first of two bills Republicans will try to pass on Wednesday to tackle voters’ concerns heading into the midterms, where President Donald Trump’s war in Iran, and its effect on the economy, could make or break the GOP’s grip on power in both chambers. DOZENS OF HOUSE DEMOCRATS REJECT BILL FUSING CONGRESSIONAL STOCK BAN WITH FEDERAL VOTER ID The stock trading bill was pushed by Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., who is in a tightening bid for re-election. The other bill will create standards for AI companies and data centers to bear the brunt of electricity costs, a key issue that has emerged in this midterm cycle that has candidates in battleground states scrambling to craft policy positions against the hulking, windowless structures. Democrats contend that the GOP's attempt to push through the data center bill is nothing more than a political lifeline for Husted's campaign. "Both pieces of legislation strike at the very heart of issues that the American people care deeply about, passionately about," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "And we'll see if the Democrats are willing to take yes for an answer."

articles.title: Óskar Matute, diputado de EH Bildu: "Un avance insuficiente en vivienda, pero un punto de partida para dar el siguiente paso"
articles.standfirst: El partido vasco apoyará los decretos de vivienda al considerarlos un avance indispensable
articles.summary: El partido vasco apoyará los decretos de vivienda al considerarlos un avance indispensable
articles.body: Oskar Matute ha confirmado que EH Bildu dará su apoyo a los dos decretos sobre vivienda presentados por el Ejecutivo, argumentando la urgencia de dar respuestas inmediatas a los sectores más vulnerables. El portavoz adjunto de la formación en el Congreso ha valorado las medidas adoptadas como un paso necesario, aunque ha insistido en que no suponen la solución definitiva al problema. Según ha explicado el diputado, "es un avance, un avance insuficiente, pero un punto de partida para dar el siguiente paso". En su intervención, comparó la situación actual con un ascenso de montaña: "Esto es un campamento base más elevado que el que transitábamos en la actualidad, pero está lejos todavía de la cima que pretendemos alcanzar". El representante de la coalición soberanista justificó la postura favorable de su grupo por el impacto directo que estas decisiones tienen sobre miles de ciudadanos con dificultades de acceso a la vivienda. "Las miles de personas y familias que en peor situación se encuentran, somos conscientes de que necesitan estas medidas y queremos poder ofrecérselas", afirmó Matute, añadiendo a continuación: "Es por eso que apoyaremos ambos decretos". No obstante, advirtió de que este respaldo no implica renunciar a reformas de mayor calado: "Hacerlo no puede suponer que renunciemos a las medidas estructurales que enfrentan realmente la emergencia habitacional que viven millones de personas". Oskar Matute reiteró la postura pragmática de su partido al equilibrar la necesidad inmediata con la exigencia de transformaciones más profundas. "Repito, somos claros: no es lo que queríamos, pero creemos que este decreto de emergencia ayudará a paliar de manera inmediata las dificultades que miles de familias y personas padecen" Asimismo, subrayó el deber de la clase política ante la ciudadanía: "Nuestra responsabilidad es ofrecer soluciones a la ciudadanía. ¿Es suficiente? No. ¿Es necesario? Sí. Jamás vamos a anteponer nuestro cálculo a las necesidades de la gente, a las necesidades del pueblo". El diputado fijó como meta principal la consolidación del derecho a un hogar digno al margen de especulaciones. "Nuestro objetivo ha sido y es enfrentar la emergencia habitacional y ofrecer soluciones reales para asegurar a la ciudadanía el acceso a viviendas dignas, estables y asequibles que acaben con el negocio y el mercado especulativo actual". En este sentido, reclamó un despliegue territorial completo de la normativa: "Para ello, creemos que será necesario que todo nuestro país, que Araba, Vizcaya, Guipúzcoa y Nafarroa sean declaradas zonas tensionadas para que todas y cada una de las herramientas se puedan aplicar y llevar a efecto". Por último, Matute concluyó su comparecencia haciendo un llamamiento a la movilización y a la perseverancia social para lograr cambios de mayor alcance. "Ese es nuestro compromiso", aseveró, antes de concluir: "Por eso, animamos a todos y a todas a que no decaigan en el ánimo, a que sigan empujando y trabajando para avanzar, para lograrlo todo, para vencer las resistencias y los miedos de quienes siempre encuentran dificultades para ir más allá".

articles.title: US FCC chair says government ads featuring Trump do not raise concerns
articles.summary: By David Shepardson WASHINGTON, Sept 30 (Reuters) - The chair of the Federal Communications Commission said on Wednesday that taxpayer-funded television ads...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept 30 (Reuters) - The chair of the Federal Communications Commission said on Wednesday that taxpayer-funded television ads featuring President ‌Donald Trump are not improper and do not raise any ‌red flags.

Democratic lawmakers said the White House transferred $20 million in Homeland Security Department funds to air ​the ads, including one that closely resembles a 2024 Trump campaign ad.

"There's nothing in there that strikes me to merit any sort of FCC review or any liability for any broadcaster for running a regular, normal (public service announcement)," FCC ‌Chair Brendan Carr, a ⁠Republican who was named head of the agency by Trump in January 2025, said.

Ethics experts and lawmakers from both parties ⁠have criticized the three nationally broadcast ads, which celebrate a "golden age of America" and are airing five weeks before midterm elections.

Lawmakers have questioned whether public funds are ​being ​used to promote Trump politically, while other ​critics say the spots may ‌violate longstanding restrictions on government propaganda and political activity.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, a Democrat, criticized the ads. "This administration has launched an aggressive effort to influence the outcome of the midterm elections," Gomez said.

The White House has defended the spots as "public service announcements" intended to promote patriotism rather than campaign ads.

Public ‌Citizen filed a complaint with the FCC ​arguing the spots are campaign advertisements that should ​not be produced or distributed ​with taxpayer resources.

One ad features Trump declaring that "America will never ‌be a communist country" while a ​chorus repeats the ​words "love me." Another combines images of Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising a "golden age of America." A third describes a "final battle" against ​the "deep state" and closely ‌resembles one of Trump's 2024 campaign advertisements.

The ads end with a ​disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government.

(Reporting by ​David Shepardson; editing by David Gaffen)

articles.title: Em meio à crise interna, ministros do STF participam de sessão
articles.summary: Supremo enfrenta 'guerra de decisões' entre os ministros. Após embate entre Moraes e Mendonça, disputa agora envolve posts sobre Nossa Senhora Aparecida.
articles.body:
Supremo enfrenta 'guerra de decisões' entre os ministros. Após embate entre Moraes e Mendonça, disputa agora envolve posts sobre Nossa Senhora Aparecida.

Os ministros do STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) se reúnem nesta quarta-feira (30) para analisar uma ação sobre planos de saúde.

A sessão ocorre em meio a seguidas crises entre os ministros. Os embates geraram uma ' guerra de decisões ' na Corte.

A nova disputa envolve os posts sobre Flávio Bolsonaro e a Nossa Senhora Aparecida. O caso está em votação no TSE.

Após a fala de Gonet, Fachin lê a pauta. Iniciando pelo recurso extraordinário 1050597.

A discussão pretende decidir se servidores públicos municipais, estaduais e distritais que ingressaram no serviço público federal, após a criação do regime de previdência complementar, podem optar pelo regime anterior.

Após o ministo Gilmar Mendes, quem pede a palavra é o Procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet.

"Senhor Presidente. Neste segundo ano do seu mandato, que se inicia às vésperas de eleições gerais em um contexto que continuará a exigir do tribunal equilíbrio e firmeza tem a convicção de que Vossa Excelência seguirá fortalecendo esta corte com a serenidade, o rigor e a retidão que marcam sua vida pública, com vistas a aprimorar o serviço que ela presta ao povo brasileiro e de que encontrará em seus pares o apoio necessário para essa. Receba, ministro Fachin, o reconhecimento desse Plenário e os meus cumprimentos pelo transcurso exitoso desse primeiro ano à frente desta corte. Muito Obrigado " , concluiu Gilmar Mendes

Em sua fala, Gilmar Mendes continua relembrando os acontecimentos dos últimos 12 meses. Segundo ele, no primeiro semestre de 2026, o plenário julgou o dobro de processos em relação ao mesmo período de 2025."

O ministro Gilmar Mendes fala sobre o 1º ano de Edson Fachin na presidência do STF. Cita a condução do colega, divergência entre eles, mas diz que essa diferença jamais alcançou aquilo que os unia: "a convicção de que o juiz não é parte nem instrumento de causa alguma".

Gilmar continua, dessa vez citando vazamentos que ele chama de seletivos. "A convicção de que o juiz não é parte, nem instrumento de causa alguma. Naquela quadra, Ministro Fachin, não houve notícias de vazamentos seletivos em nossos gabinetes – apesar da sensibilidade dos documentos que estavam sob nossa responsabilidade – tampouco qualquer ato que pudesse indicar uso políticoeleitoral das investigações. Discordamos no resultado; nunca na equidistância que deve guiar a postura de qualquer magistrado" , disse.

articles.title: Senate Democrats block Sen. Husted-led bill on data centers, calling it ‘toothless’
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities. The vote was 57-43, short of the 60 needed to break a filibuster. The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House by a vote of 417-3 two weeks ago, sets a federal standard on the issue. It also instructs state public utility commissions to find ways to make developers of data centers that use huge amounts of energy cover their own costs of water and electricity to consumers. The Senate version is led by appointed Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who’s locked in a competitive battle as he seeks his first full Senate term. He’s facing heat at home from Democratic rival and former senator Sherrod Brown, who has branded him “the face of data centers” for promoting developments when he was lieutenant governor. “I heard they said they wanted lower electricity prices,” Husted said of Democrats on Tuesday. “All they have to do is not block it, vote for it, and it will be on the president’s desk, and we will have a bipartisan win.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the bill is merely “optional” for states and won’t achieve much beyond partisan messaging for Republicans. “Plain and simple, the Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday. “It does not require any protections at all. While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill. We need real action on data centers.” Schumer said Republicans should instead take up bills by Sens. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., that would go further in imposing cost-related rules on data centers. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., rejected Democratic arguments that the bill is simply a Republican political move to protect Husted’s re-election bid. He noted that nearly every House Democrat voted for the measure. “I don’t know how you can say something that passed the House of Representatives 417-3 isn’t consequential,” Thune told reporters. “AOC voted for it over there. Hakeem Jeffries voted for it over there. This is a bill that could go to the president and become law. Evidently, a lot of Democrats in the House of Representatives thought it was important to be for and thought that it did exactly what the bill says it does.” An NBC News poll this month found that data centers are unpopular: By nearly 6 to 1, voters said they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports building a data center in their community. The survey found that voters trust Democrats over Republicans by a margin of 12 points to deal with data centers. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring, said Husted was “right to get the message out” on data center costs. But when asked if the bill would achieve much beyond that, Tillis said, “No.” “I think the best way to deal with this is ... down in North Carolina, most utilities are managed through public utility commissions,” Tillis said. “They’re managed through local and state decision-making. That’s where it should be.”

articles.title: Dems kill Republican's chances of lowering Americans' electricity bills in key election flashpoint
articles.summary: Senate Democrats blocked the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill aimed at making AI data centers bear rising electricity costs that Jon Husted championed.
articles.body: Democrats blocked a push to tackle one of the key issues driving this midterm election cycle, and may have given a vulnerable Republican a political lifeline in the process. Republicans’ effort to crack down on rising electricity costs caused by the boom in data centers across the country was stifled on Wednesday by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats, despite cruising through the House in a massive bipartisan vote. Schumer’s blockade, however, wasn't unanimous among Democrats, with four — Sens. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., and Maggie Hassan, D-N.H. — breaking ranks to support the bill. The Ratepayer Protection Act, would have created a standard for AI companies and the data centers they run to bear the brunt of electricity costs — an issue that has become a predominant concern for voters this midterm cycle. FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY But Democrats argued it was a toothless effort that lacked any real enforcement mechanism, and merely a political ploy to give vulnerable Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, a boost. "The Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud. It does not require any protections at all," Schumer said. "While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill." "We need real action on data centers. And what do Republicans decide all of a sudden to push force forward a bill that is totally optional?" While the U.S. continues its arms race with China for AI dominance, voters want to see tech companies cool their jets and slow the rapid construction of data centers. A Fox News poll from July found that 70% of voters, both Republicans and Democrats, opposed the construction of new data centers. SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS Republicans, including Husted, hoped that voter concerns could persuade Democrats to break from Schumer and vote in favor of the bill heading into Wednesday’s test. "We all know that people would like to see us do something to lower their prices," Husted said. We have the opportunity to do that." Data centers have become a political cudgel against Husted in his race against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who has labeled him the "face of data centers" in a battle that could determine who wins the majority in November. Husted argued that the bill passed the House with only three Democrats voting against it, and that this push didn’t need to be labeled a "partisan victory." Killing the bill, however, could give Husted a needed boost to campaign on, given that Democrats stopped one of the main issues voters have going into the election, particularly in Ohio. "It's like, look, this can be an opportunity for the Democrats to join us and say, ‘yeah, we agree. We're gonna work with them to get something done,’ and I hope they will," Husted said. ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER But Democrats countered the legislation was just a stunt to give Husted political ammunition. Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital that voters could see through the politics being played with by the GOP, and that the bill is "good for Senator Husted, but not necessarily for them." "Because it's not, it doesn't have anything that would actually force change," Kim said. "And so that's what we need. We need something that is actually gonna be substantial and meet the moment rather than things that are just designed to be able to help with political elections." "I just think, if you’re looking at issues that we want to get at the heart of what everybody seems to be saying, the Democrats and others are saying, are important, we're concerned about," Thune said. "And it's a chance to actually make the law, it’s not just making a point here."

articles.title: Republican glee erupts as White House boasts sharp decline in immigration from Muslim-majority nations
articles.summary: A White House graph shows a 96% drop in legal immigration from Muslim-majority nations since 2024, but the Cato researcher behind it pushed back.
articles.body: The political right celebrated after a White House X account posted a graph showing that legal immigration to the U.S. from nations with Muslim majority populations has all but halted. The account highlighted a 96 percent cut in legal immigration from majority-Muslim countries since 2024 and attached a graph from the Cato Institute, a notoriously pro-immigration think tank. The graph showed a drastic decline in quarterly admissions of immigrants from those countries beginning in January 2025, when President Donald Trump officially took office. It also declined in late 2024, the last year of former President Joe Biden's tenure in office. AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION At its peak, immigration from Muslim-majority nations was over 22,000 people per month between July and October of 2024, according to the graph. But by the beginning of January of this year, that number had dropped to almost zero. Online, the political right cheered the drastic shift. "Absolutely incredible victory for the American people, thanks to POTUS," Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, said. "These are the wins we need to continue to deliver on," said Brandon Herrera, the GOP nominee for Congress in Texas' 23rd District. "4 percent to go! Thank you, President Trump," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "Let’s pump up those rookie numbers for every category of immigrant," columnist Kurt Schlichter said. 100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY Some turned the graph into a referendum on the results of Republican leadership, and urged conservatives to vote during the 2026 midterm elections despite concerns about cost-of-living, the Iran war, and other issues for which Trump has been knocked by members of his own party. "I voted for this—and will again," said user David Harrison. "The next time you get the urge to 'punish the GOP.' Remember that Democrats will reverse this overnight," said Turning Point Action's Ben Larrabee. "People screaming that Trump and the GOP aren't doing anything about this problem [are] hardest hit, like squarely between the eyes," online personality James Lindsay said of the graph. JONATHAN TURLEY: SUPREME COURT HANDS TRUMP A BORDER VICTORY LIBERALS CAN'T SPIN "Vote like Western Civilization depends on it, because it does," said Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet. Not everyone was thrilled with the decline in legal immigration from this demographic, though, including David J. Bier, who is the director of immigration studies at Cato and who took credit for the research behind the graph. "Thanks for citing my work. You are violating the law and harming Americans while making the country less safe, less free, and less prosperous," he said in reply. Despite Bier's claim, no court has decided that Trump's move to reduce immigration from Muslim-majority countries is "illegal," though there have been challenges in district courts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP During his first term in office, Trump faced a challenge to his proposed travel restrictions from Muslim-majority countries. The policy was enjoined by the federal district court for the District of Hawaii, and upheld by two federal appellate courts. However, the Supreme Court ultimately decided in Hawaii vs. Trump that Trump's policy was legal.
